what_it_does: Compilers — programs that translate human-readable code into machine instructions — use a data structure called an e-graph (equality-saturation graph) to compactly represent many equivalent ways of computing the same thing, then pick the cheapest version. Choosing the best option from this graph (called extraction) is a hard combinatorial puzzle: exact algorithms are very slow on large graphs, and fast shortcuts often produce mediocre results. SmoothE reframes the problem as a continuous optimization: instead of making hard yes/no choices about which nodes to include, it assigns each node a real-valued score and smoothly adjusts all scores together using gradient descent (the same math used to train neural networks), then rounds the final scores to a definite choice. This approach also supports arbitrary cost functions — including ones learned by neural networks — rather than being limited to simple arithmetic costs.
